title: Attention Is All You Need | · | p. 1 of 15 | ∨ | Tinct text

passage: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
text:
The selected phrase means the Transformer drops both recurrent and convolutional layers, relying only on attention.

Recurrence means processing a sequence one step at a time, with each step depending on the previous hidden state. Convolutions apply a sliding window over the input. The paper, on page 1, says the Transformer is "based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely." That is the architectural claim the whole paper rests on.

Here, "dispensing with" means "doing without," so the phrase is a contrast with the prior state of the art, which the abstract describes as "complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks." Attention lets every position relate directly to every other, which is why the authors say the model is more parallelizable and faster to train.

passage: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples
text:
The selected sentence says that the sequential nature of recurrent models prevents parallel computation within a single training example p. 2.

Recurrent models compute a hidden state h_t for each position t from the previous state h_{t-1} and the input at that position. Each step must wait for the one before it, so the positions cannot be processed at the same time. This matters most for long sequences, where memory limits how many examples can be batched together p. 2.

The sentence is the motivation for the paper's design. The Transformer drops recurrence and relies on attention alone, so all positions can be computed in parallel p. 2.

passage: Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence
text:
Self-attention, also called intra-attention, is a way for a model to relate different positions within one sequence to build a representation of that sequence.

Self-attention is an attention mechanism that links different positions of a single sequence. It is sometimes called intra-attention. In other words, each part of a sentence can look at the other parts of the same sentence. The model uses these links to represent the whole sequence. This is the idea the passage introduces on page 2 p. 2.

passage: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
text:
The model can use several attention heads at once, so it looks at information from different representation subspaces and different positions together.

Multi-head attention lets the model look at information from different positions and from different kinds of representation at the same time. With only one attention head, averaging would prevent this.

The passage claims the Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, beating prior results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. The document supports this with its own results table comparing BLEU scores and training costs against earlier models p. 8, and a dedicated results section stating the 28.4 score p. 8. passage: being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train
text:
The strongest objection is that the speed claim compares a parallel model against sequential baselines without matching the hardware, budgets, or training effort.

Parallelizability is a property of the architecture, but wall-clock training time depends on implementation, hardware, batch size, and how much tuning each model received. The document's own cost figures rest on estimates: it says training FLOPs were estimated by multiplying training time, GPU count, and an assumed sustained throughput for each GPU p. 8. A critic could argue that the reported advantage therefore mixes architectural gains with engineering choices, and that a fairly tuned recurrent model on the same hardware might narrow the gap. The document also reports only a few baselines in its cost table, so the comparison does not cover every alternative.

The author's best reply is that the Transformer's constant number of sequential operations per layer allows far more parallel computation during training, and that it reaches higher BLEU at a fraction of the cost of the compared models p. 8.

question: Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?
text:
The document only gives the cause and the footnote's setup, not the full mechanism, so part of this is my own explanation from general knowledge.

What the document says: for large dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, which pushes the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients p. 4. Footnote 4 explains why they grow: if the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance dk p. 4. So its typical size scales like √dk, which is why they divide by √dk.

The gradient step is not spelled out, but from general knowledge: softmax turns scores into weights that sum to 1. When one score is much larger than the others, the output saturates, with one weight near 1 and the rest near 0. In that saturated regime, small changes to the scores barely change the weights, so the gradient, which involves products like p(1−p), is close to zero. Learning through the attention weights then becomes very slow. Scaling keeps the scores at roughly unit variance, so the softmax stays in a more responsive range.

The authors call this a suspicion, not something they test directly in the paper.

Before you start
×

The paper proposes the Transformer, a translation architecture built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It matters because it aims for better quality and far faster parallel training, and the rest of the paper describes, motivates and tests that design.

Key claims

1
The Transformer relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. p. 2
2
Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations, versus O(n) for recurrent layers. p. 6
3
The big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating prior results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. p. 8
4
Ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. p. 9
5
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs well on English constituency parsing, including with only 40K WSJ training sentences. p. 10

Keep in mind

The English-to-French big model score appears as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but as 41.0 in the text of section 6.1. Check which figure you rely on.
Attention itself is not new. The novelty claimed is using it without recurrent or convolutional layers, so read the Background section with that distinction in mind.
Perplexities in Table 3 are per-wordpiece under byte-pair encoding, so they should not be compared with per-word perplexities from other work. Training cost figures are estimates built from GPU time and assumed sustained TFLOPS.
